A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EBD research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered between versions.

before.justification: v1 reports original MNIST and CIFAR-10 training results, learning curves, runtime measurements, and activation–error correlation analyses in Section 4 and Appendices H–I.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds 10-layer CorInfoMax-EBD results and gradient-alignment measurements in Appendix E.

M1.justification: The core EBD objectives, local updates, regularizers, and CorInfoMax integration are retained. For the new 10-layer experiments, Appendix I.3.7 adds periodic weight thresholding every 5,000 samples, setting weights at a specified scale relative to the peak to zero. This is a limited training-procedure adaptation.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate MNIST and CIFAR-10 image classification. The added depth experiments and gradient diagnostics use retained datasets and tasks; they introduce no new domain, population, or input scenario.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark comparisons retain BP, DFA, DFA+E, NN-GEVB, and MS-GEVB for MLP/CNN/LC networks, and CorInfoMax-EP for CorInfoMax-EBD. Runtime comparison sets also remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds 10-layer, batch-size-one CorInfoMax evaluations and cosine-similarity protocols for gradient diagnostics. It also distinguishes 60-epoch training for the 3-layer batch-size-20 model from 30 epochs for batch size one, whereas v1 states 60 epochs for CorInfoMax generally. These are substantial additions and revisions to reported settings, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix E tests whether EBD updates align with BP gradients in CIFAR-10 MLP and LC networks, and whether retaining only the local gradient component preserves alignment with the full decorrelation gradient. These directly investigate previously untested optimization and truncation questions. The 10-layer experiments additionally examine depth feasibility.

E5.justification: v2 Tables 1–2 add numerical ± values to original accuracy results; v1 tables report means alone, although shaded learning curves already appear. Both versions state five repetitions. v2 does not identify the ± quantities as standard deviations, standard errors, or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: v2 adds 10-layer accuracies of 96.4±0.11% on MNIST and 54.9±0.58% on CIFAR-10, predominantly positive gradient-alignment findings, and replacement CorInfoMax accuracy curves under different settings. Some existing displayed means also change beyond rounding: CIFAR-10 LC EBD changes from 64.23 to 64.3, batch-size-20 CorInfoMax-EBD from 55.79 to 55.7, and online MNIST CorInfoMax-EBD from 94.7 to 94.9. Most other benchmark means are equivalent after rounding.

T1.justification: v1 provides MMSE lemmas and motivates hidden-unit orthogonality constraints. v2 Appendix B adds Theorem B.1 proving the converse orthogonality characterization and Theorem B.2 presenting a conditional infinite-width convergence argument. The latter assumes dense first-layer features and exact orthogonality, with bounded error used in the proof. These substantially expand the formal theoretical treatment.

C1.justification: The central claims about decorrelation-based error broadcasting and biological learning remain. v2's introduction and conclusion additionally claim demonstrated training of deep recurrent biologically plausible networks and initial depth scalability, whereas v1 leaves scalability unvalidated.

C2.justification: v2 interprets gradient alignment as support for local truncation and explicitly discusses the idealized feature-richness assumptions and unresolved preservation of universality during training. It replaces v1's speculative scalability analogy with DFA by a bounded interpretation of the 10-layer evidence. The earlier Appendix B.4 discussion suggesting analogous implicit regularization is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds a 10-layer hyperparameter table and thresholding instructions, dataset access and licensing statements, and computational-resource details. Appendix I.10 specifies a single 32-GB V100 and approximate training times of 22 and 75 hours for the described configurations. Existing implementation descriptions and supplementary-code access statements are largely retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references to Makur, Rahimi and Recht, and Sun et al. for the MMSE and random-feature arguments, plus LeCun and Cortes for MNIST provenance. It removes the Soudry citation with the implicit-regularization discussion. The broader positioning against existing credit-assignment methods remains stable.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, theoretical motivation, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Biological-plausibility explanations are condensed, Appendix B is reorganized, and the separate impact statement is integrated into Section 5. Citation style also changes from author–year to numbered references.

P2.justification: v2 introduces three multipanel gradient-diagnostic figures, replaces two CorInfoMax accuracy panels with 10-layer curves, merges the two dataset-specific benchmark tables, and adds a depth column and hyperparameter table. Figure 1 is resized and its caption shortened. These materially change the visual presentation beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central local-update mechanism: Appendix E directly examines the gradient truncation adopted in v1, while Appendix B makes conditions for the MMSE interpretation explicit. The 10-layer experiments replace speculative depth scalability with concrete feasibility evidence, and uncertainty and resource disclosures improve assessment. Undefined ± quantities and the retained 55.79% text versus 55.7% table discrepancy limit reporting quality, but the added support for key methodological choices provides a substantial net improvement.
